## Openings by genre convention

### Name the Promise Before the Move

**Also called:** the opening selector, promise before move, what are you actually opening
**What it is:** The card at the head of the `open.` shelf. It does not describe an opening. It asks — in order — **which of this shelf's two decisions you are making**, then **what the first thing the audience is given is**, **how much of the promise is said out loud**, and **whether this is first contact at all** — and hands back a named shortlist for each answer. The axes were not invented: they were read off the shelf's own `Yields to:` conditions and cross-checked against `Avoid when:`, and the conditions that repeated became the questions. Every card cited here is cited by id.
**Effect on the audience:** None. This card never reaches the page or the screen. It exists so that the opening that does reach them was chosen against the promise the piece intends to keep, rather than picked because it was the last good opening the writer read.
**Used for and where it works best:** **Write the promise first, in one sentence, before you open the shelf** — *"this is a story about a family, told from the outside"*, *"you have been told the wrong century about this arch"*. Then answer the questions in order, out loud, one sentence each. The first fork sends whole regions of the shelf away; the next two leave a shortlist of three to six. **If you cannot write the promise, you are not ready to open — you are ready to find out what the piece is**, and `open.logline_diagnostic` is the tool for that, not this one. Where two promises fight for one opening, that is two pieces — or a piece and its packaging, and `open.visual_promise` says which of those two the audience will believe.
**Best in:** formats: all | genres: all
**Avoid when:** **The opening already exists and the note on it is "it doesn't work."** That is a diagnosis, not a choice, and it is rarely answered on this shelf: a broken opening is usually a broken ending, an unpaid promise or a missing character, and the repair lives in `end.`, `arc.` or `char.`. Also avoid it wherever the piece's whole value is that its opening is unlike any named opening — this map returns named moves, and a shelf of named moves run straight produces work that is competent and recognisable. And **distrust anything this map appears to send you to by way of a card's prose rather than by way of its `Yields to:` field.** This shelf carries both shapes and they read identically: a card naming the working alternative, and a card naming the failure it becomes when done badly. One pair of ids carries both directions at once — `open.overload_open` names `open.first_paragraph_contents` as the budget that prevents it, and `open.first_paragraph_contents` names `open.overload_open` as what happens without it. **Follow the second as if it were the first and you have chosen a named failure on purpose.** Only the `Yields to:` field is a route. Everything else in a card's prose is a warning, a companion or a repair.
**Example:**
> **Promise:** *a heritage documentary, and the land is the antagonist.*
> Which decision: the piece itself, not its packaging. First thing given: a place and the way it works. Said out loud: withheld entirely. First contact: yes.
> **Shortlist:** `open.weather_open` · `open.rule_of_the_world` · `open.last_ordinary_day` — and the shelf files the first of those under its own failures, which is the point of the next field but one.

---

**The axes**

**Axis one, asked before any of the others — which of this shelf's two decisions are you making?** Almost everything filed under `open.` is about the first minutes of the piece. A smaller region is about **what the audience meets before the piece begins**: the cover, the thumbnail, the title, the logline, the first page of a pitch. Those are decided at a different moment, about a different artefact, and judged by a different number — `open.package_undersell` is the card that separates them, and it separates them mechanically: *low open rate with high completion means the package is wrong; high open rate with early drop-off means the opening is wrong*, and *"fixing the second when you have the first wastes months"*. The pair graph agrees with it. **Not one `Yields to:` field on this shelf crosses between the two regions in either direction.** Every packaging card names another packaging card; every opening card names another opening card.

**Axis two — what is the first thing the audience is given?** Eight of the shelf's conditions turn on it, and they are stated as facts rather than as feelings: *"Plot-forward genre work, reader came for the machine"* (`open.character_hook`), *"First act is genuinely slow, not fast"* (`open.situation_hook`), *"The show is about the investigators, not the cases"* (`open.procedural_body`), *"Open on the job, not the hiring"* (`open.crew_assembly`), *"Shrink to one person the audience can attach to"* (`open.unearned_stakes`), *"Character-led comedy, where the engine is a person"* (`open.comedy_premise_statement`), *"Protagonist is a veteran; no newcomer to learn through"* (`open.war_arrival`), *"Literary work where the place is the subject and prose is the hook"* (`open.weather_open`). One card on the shelf exists to state this axis rather than to answer it — `open.information_order`: *whichever element appears first is what you have promised the book is about*.

**Axis three — how much of the promise is said out loud, and who says it?** This is the condition the shelf repeats most: fifteen of its `Yields to:` lines turn on it, and four of them name the fork in the cards' own words. *"Drama, where a spoken promise becomes a summary"* (`open.stated_promise`), *"Drama, where a narrator must ask the audience nothing"* (`open.opening_question_line`), *"Fiction, where the stake cannot be stated in the writer's voice"* (`open.nut_graf`), *"Narration is carrying exposition a scene should demonstrate"* (`open.voiceover_open`), *"Name the gap rather than announce the thesis"* (`open.documentary_open`), *"The withheld thing is atmospheric, not verifiable"* (`open.mystery_discovery`), *"The rupture must stay a surprise, unsignalled"* (`open.last_ordinary_day`), *"Psychological horror, threat must stay ambiguous"* (`open.horror_cold_open`).

**Axis four — is this first contact, or does the audience already carry something of this work?** Nine conditions are about arrival rather than about content: *"Episodic work that resets, no distance to measure"* (`open.opening_image_answered`), *"The first episode, which carries a second job"* (`open.episode_opening`), *"The world is the audience's own"* (`open.rule_of_the_world`), *"Audience already has the question; name the deliverable"* (`open.explainer_promise`), *"Instructional writing, where a doorway is friction"* (`open.essay_first_move`), *"The returning player, or systems too complex to gate"* (`open.tutorial_as_scene`), *"The history is needed; offset it in time or register"* (`open.backstory_open`). **It is asked last because all but seven of the reachable cards sit under its first value** — so on a standalone piece this map has two questions left, not three. But when the honest answer is not *first contact*, it is the only axis here that eliminates anything at all.

**The default, and the one against it**

**The default is `open.character_hook` carrying who arrives, with `open.question_planted_first` carrying what is withheld — a specific person, and one thing about them nobody has explained. It is measured, not asserted.** Four cards tie at the top of this shelf's in-degree, each named by three others: `open.character_hook`, `open.question_planted_first`, `open.ordinary_day_slightly_wrong` and `open.stated_promise`. Two of those four break the tie. **`open.question_planted_first` is the only card on the shelf reached from three different regions of it** — from the first-page hooks (`open.situation_hook`, *"First act is genuinely slow, not fast"*), from the genre conventions (`open.mystery_discovery`, *"The withheld thing is atmospheric, not verifiable"*) and from the non-fiction block (`open.nut_graf`, *"Fiction, where the stake cannot be stated in the writer's voice"*). **`open.character_hook` is the shelf's repair address** — the only card named by a card the package files as a failure, and three cards send a reader there when their own move has collapsed: `open.unearned_stakes` (*"Shrink to one person the audience can attach to"*), `open.procedural_body` (*"The show is about the investigators, not the cases"*) and `open.comedy_premise_statement` (*"Character-led comedy, where the engine is a person"*). Asked over and over where to fall back to, the shelf falls back to a person and a question about them. Which is also why it is the most worn opening in the drawer.

**The one against it is `open.weather_open`, and choosing it is a deliberate refusal of the default.** It is the only card here that declines to put a person in the audience's hands at all, and it declines on purpose, for the two cases its own card names: literary work where the place *is* the subject, and heritage or nature work where the landscape is the protagonist. Three things make it an against-the-grain choice rather than a mistake. **Nothing routes to it** — no `Yields to:` field on the shelf names it, and the one card that mentions it, `open.information_order`, mentions it as *the standard failure of this decision*, which is a pointer and not a route, so the pair graph can only ever send a reader away from it. **The shelf files it under its own failures and the package does not agree** — every card the package actually marks as a failure carries the banner *and* an empty `Best in:` line, and the two agree on every one of them; `open.weather_open` carries neither, and lists real formats and real genres, heritage and nature among them. And **its cost is stated and payable**: if the first person has not appeared by the third paragraph, move them to the first. Its near cousin against the grain is `open.loop_opening`, likewise never yielded to by anything, and the only card on the shelf whose opening is authored backwards from the ending rather than forwards from a blank page.

---

**The unasked**

**Twenty-nine of the shelf's reachable cards are the target of no `Yields to:` field anywhere on it.** They can be chosen, but nothing ever sends you to them. By id:

`open.opening_image_answered` · `open.theme_stated_early` · `open.title_delayed` · `open.scale_reveal` · `open.first_second_hook` · `open.loop_opening` · `open.false_start` · `open.backstory_open` · `open.weather_open` · `open.unearned_stakes` · `open.chapter_opening` · `open.scene_opening` · `open.horror_cold_open` · `open.the_meet` · `open.crew_assembly` · `open.procedural_body` · `open.war_arrival` · `open.framing_prologue` · `open.opening_question_line` · `open.information_order` · `open.title_changes_meaning` · `open.logline_diagnostic` · `open.broken_logline_reading` · `open.pitch_first_page` · `open.documentary_open` · `open.essay_first_move` · `open.tutorial_as_scene` · `open.first_choice` · `open.nut_graf`

**And the shape of that list is the finding, not its length.** Almost every card on it has one property in common: **it is not complete until a second moment elsewhere in the piece answers it.** `open.opening_image_answered` needs the mirrored final image. `open.loop_opening` needs the ending to join to. `open.theme_stated_early` needs the ending to measure against. `open.title_delayed` needs the turn the card lands on. `open.framing_prologue` needs the return to the frame. `open.crew_assembly` needs every demonstrated skill redeemed. `open.horror_cold_open` needs later scenes to read against its rule. `open.the_meet` needs the flaw repaired. `open.procedural_body` needs its anomaly to become the episode's subject. `open.first_choice` needs to be visibly acknowledged hours later. `open.nut_graf` needs a lede in front of it, and `open.essay_first_move` needs its turn a few paragraphs on. **A card whose whole content is a contract with a later moment has no rival at minute one — its rival is at minute ninety**, and the pair field, written by a reader holding one card at one moment, cannot express that. A stated promise is not an alternative to a withheld one; it is a different kind of answer. That is why axis four is on this card and why it is asked last rather than not at all.

The second thing the list shows: **every card that names the kind of piece it belongs to is a source and never a destination.** Horror, romance, heist, procedural, war, documentary, essay, journalism, game, pitch — the whole genre-convention region and the whole non-fiction region yield outward and nothing yields inward. The reason is direction. A reader holding `open.horror_cold_open` can name the general fallback for when the threat must stay ambiguous; a reader holding the general card cannot name every genre that specialises it, because those are not alternatives to it — they are the same move performed inside a convention. **The pair graph runs from the specific to the general and never back**, so the specific end of this shelf is reachable only by knowing what kind of piece you are making before you open it. That is exactly what axis two's last value and axis four's last two values are for.

And the card this shelf wants and does not have: **the one that says the opening's job is to name the debt and the ending's job is to pay it.** The shelf records the failure of that contract in full — `open.abandoned_device`, *any device introduced in an opening must appear at least twice more, and one of those appearances should be near the end* — and records the working version nowhere, in no card, while more than twenty of its cards quietly depend on it. The nearest thing that exists is a failure card explaining the rule it is the violation of, with nothing routing a reader from any of those twenty to it.

`open.promise_before_the_move`

### The Horror Cold Open

**Also called:** the pre-title kill, the demonstration victim
**What it is:** A short self-contained sequence, usually before the title, in which the threat is demonstrated on someone the audience has just met and will not see again.
**Effect on the audience:** They learn the rules of the danger while the protagonist is still safe, which converts every later ordinary scene into suspense. The whole first act then runs on dread the opening bought.
**Used for and where it works best:** Horror features, horror series, and thrillers with a standing threat. The craft rule that separates the good version from the cheap one: the opening must teach a *rule*, not just show a death. If the audience leaves it knowing the thing only comes at night, or only when you say the name, every later scene can be read against that rule. A kill that teaches nothing is a trailer moment stapled to the front. Pair with `tens.threat_with_rules` and `tens.dread_over_shock`; it is a specialised case of `open.cold_open`.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Limited Series, Short Film, Series, Game Narrative | genres: Horror, Thriller, Mystery, Crime, Science Fiction
**Avoid when:** The film's real subject is psychological and the threat is meant to stay ambiguous — a demonstrated monster kills ambiguity permanently. Also avoid when the victim is written purely as meat; an audience that feels nothing for the first death has been trained to feel nothing for the rest.
**Example:**
> She locks the car door. Then the other three, one at a time, out loud: "Two. Three. Four."
> Nothing comes. She starts the engine. The interior light says the boot is open.

**Yields to:** `open.ordinary_day_slightly_wrong` — Psychological horror, threat must stay ambiguous.  
`open.horror_cold_open`

### The Meet

**Also called:** the meet-cute, the first collision, the romance inciting encounter
**What it is:** The two people who will end up together meet, early, under circumstances that force them into contact and put them immediately at odds.
**Effect on the audience:** The contract is signed in one scene — the audience now knows the shape of the whole piece and settles in to enjoy the route rather than the destination.
**Used for and where it works best:** Romance and romantic comedy in every format, and any story with a central pairing, including buddy films and heist duos. The rule: the meeting must generate a *reason they cannot simply proceed*. Charm is not enough — the scene works when it establishes friction that will take the whole story to resolve. The strongest version also reveals each character's flaw to the other in the first sixty seconds, so the ending can be its repair. In vertical micro-drama and reels the meet still obeys `open.open_mid_situation`: no arrival and no greeting — open inside the collision, as the example does, with the two already at odds.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Half-Hour Comedy, Novel, Vertical Micro-Drama, Limited Series, Reels/Shorts, Stage Play | genres: Romance, Comedy, Drama, Coming of Age, Family Drama
**Avoid when:** The relationship is meant to feel inevitable rather than chosen, or when the pairing is not the story's engine. Also avoid in a piece where the two have a long history — there, the meeting has already happened and the opening's job is the reunion, which is a different scene entirely.
**Example:**
> "You're in my seat."
> "I'm in seat 14A."
> "I know. I'm in 14A."

**Yields to:** `rel.reunion_after_separation` — The two have a long history; the meeting already happened.  
`open.the_meet`

### The Crew Assembly

**Also called:** the team gather, getting the band together, the heist recruit
**What it is:** The opening introduces the plan by introducing the people needed to execute it, each brought in through a scene that demonstrates their single specific competence.
**Effect on the audience:** Pleasure of anticipation. Every skill shown in the assembly becomes a promise the audience waits to see redeemed.
**Used for and where it works best:** Heist, caper, war, sports and any ensemble mission story. The craft rule is one-competence-per-person, demonstrated not stated — a character introduced picking a lock is a locksmith forever, a character introduced being *called* a locksmith is a name. Cap the recruits at about five before the plan; more than that and the audience stops tracking who does what, which is `open.overload_open` in costume. Every skill established here must be used, and the best structures make one of them fail at the worst moment.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Limited Series, Game Narrative, Animation Feature, One-Hour Drama, Novel | genres: Heist, Crime, War, Adventure, Comedy, Science Fiction, Thriller
**Avoid when:** The story is about the plan going wrong from the inside, where a long assembly makes the audience invest in a team the story intends to betray. Also avoid when the crew is the second act's business — some stories open on the job, not the hiring.
**Example:**
> "What do you do?"
> The old man takes the visitor's watch off his own wrist and hands it back to him.
> "That. Mostly that."

**Yields to:** `open.situation_hook` — Open on the job, not the hiring.  
`open.crew_assembly`

### The Body on Page One

**Also called:** the procedural corpse, the case arrives, the crime open
**What it is:** The crime, incident or case that the episode will solve arrives in the first minutes, usually before anyone the audience knows is present.
**Effect on the audience:** A frame to hang everything on. The audience immediately knows the shape of the hour, which frees the writer to spend the middle on character.
**Used for and where it works best:** Procedural television above all, plus crime novels, medical drama and any case-of-the-week form. The convention is settled enough that breaking it costs more than keeping it. The differentiation is not *whether* the body arrives but *what is wrong with it* — one anomalous detail in the opening becomes the episode's actual subject. In series with a standing arc, the body's detail should also touch the season question, which is how procedural episodes carry serial weight.
**Best in:** formats: One-Hour Drama, Series, Novel, Limited Series, Podcast, Short Story | genres: Procedural, Crime, Mystery, Thriller, Medical, Legal
**Avoid when:** The show is about the investigators rather than the cases, where a cold case-open teaches the audience to wait for the wrong thing. Also avoid in a first episode where the world needs establishing before the machine starts.
**Example:**
> The dead man is wearing someone else's shoes. Correct size. Bought that week. Not his.

**Yields to:** `open.character_hook` — The show is about the investigators, not the cases.  
`open.procedural_body`

### The Arrival

**Also called:** the war open, the newcomer's first day, the deployment beat
**What it is:** The story opens with a character arriving into the world of the piece — a front, a camp, a ward, a prison, a country — so that the audience learns the place at the character's speed.
**Effect on the audience:** Orientation with tension attached. They are ignorant alongside someone who is about to be punished for being ignorant.
**Used for and where it works best:** War, migration, institutional drama, heritage and any closed world with rules. The rule that makes it work: the arriving character must already *want something*, or the opening becomes a tour. And the place must correct them within the first scene — the veteran who tells them what they got wrong is the scene's real engine, not the geography. See `expo.newcomer_eye` for the exposition mechanics and `char.audience_surrogate_trap` for the risk.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Limited Series, Novel, One-Hour Drama, Documentary, Game Narrative, Stage Play | genres: War, Social Drama, Historical, Heritage, Migration, Drama, Science Fiction
**Avoid when:** The audience already knows the world, or the protagonist is a veteran of it — then the arrival is someone else's story. Also avoid the version where the newcomer exists only to be explained to; that is a walking question mark, not a character.
**Example:**
> "Where do I put my bag?"
> Nobody answers. He puts it on the empty bed. Three men look at the bed and then at him and then away.

**Yields to:** `open.rule_of_the_world` — Protagonist is a veteran; no newcomer to learn through.  
`open.war_arrival`

### The Premise Stated

**Also called:** the comedy set-up, the engine declared, the situation announced
**What it is:** The opening tells the audience the absurd arrangement the comedy will run on — the mismatch, the lie, the impossible job — clearly and fast, and then starts exploiting it.
**Effect on the audience:** Permission to laugh. Comedy audiences cannot relax until they know what the joke machine is, and every second spent guessing is a second not laughing.
**Used for and where it works best:** Half-hour comedy, comic features, sketch, and comic short-form. This is the place where clarity beats subtlety outright: the premise should be legible by the end of the first scene, in a sitcom by the end of the cold open. The craft is in what happens *after* the statement — the first complication should arrive within a page, proving the premise generates story rather than just a situation. Related but distinct from `open.stated_promise`, which is a non-fiction device; this one states a comic engine, not a deliverable.
**Best in:** formats: Half-Hour Comedy, Feature Film, Reels/Shorts, Web Series, Animation Feature, Stage Play | genres: Comedy, Satire, Family Drama, Romance
**Avoid when:** The comedy is character-led rather than situation-led, where the engine is a person and stating it flattens them. Also avoid in dark comedy, where the pleasure depends on the audience discovering how bad the arrangement is rather than being told.
**Example:**
> "So we're agreed. For two weeks, you're my wife, he's your brother, and none of us has ever been to Basra."
> "I've been to Basra."
> "As of this morning you haven't."

**Yields to:** `open.character_hook` — Character-led comedy, where the engine is a person.  
`open.comedy_premise_statement`

### The Discovery Open

**Also called:** the mystery's first fact, the found thing, the anomaly
**What it is:** The opening presents a discovery — a document, a discrepancy, a missing person, an object where it should not be — that the rest of the work exists to explain.
**Effect on the audience:** A licence to speculate, which is the specific pleasure mysteries sell. Unlike a question planted for atmosphere, a discovery gives the audience something to *work with*.
**Used for and where it works best:** Mystery, detective fiction, investigative documentary and narrative podcast. The rule that distinguishes it from `open.question_planted_first`: a discovery is verifiable — it is a fact the audience can hold and test against later facts, and fair-play mystery requires the audience to receive it at the same moment the detective does. State it plainly. A discovery dressed in atmosphere reads as mood and gets discarded. See `info.fair_play_contract`.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Podcast, Limited Series, Documentary, Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Short Story | genres: Mystery, Crime, Procedural, Thriller, Historical, Heritage
**Avoid when:** The discovery's explanation is mundane, or when it arrives before the audience has any frame to judge it against. In investigative non-fiction, avoid opening on a discovery you cannot substantiate later — the form's whole credit rests on it.
**Example:**
> The house had been empty for nine years. The electricity bill for last month was forty-one dinars.

**Yields to:** `open.question_planted_first` — The withheld thing is atmospheric, not verifiable.  
`open.mystery_discovery`

### The Last Ordinary Day

**Also called:** the coming-of-age open, the world about to end, the before
**What it is:** The opening shows the protagonist's life exactly as it is, in full working order, while the audience is told — by title, by narration, by structure or by genre — that it is about to stop.
**Effect on the audience:** Retrospective tenderness applied in advance. Every ordinary detail becomes precious because the audience knows it is being shown a *last*.
**Used for and where it works best:** Coming of age, heritage, family drama, war and migration stories. It is distinct from `open.ordinary_day_slightly_wrong`: nothing here is wrong, and that is the point. The craft rule is to write the day at full ordinariness, with real pleasures and real irritations, and to let the *frame* carry the dread — a retrospective narrator, a dated title card, a genre the audience already trusts. See `voice.retrospective_narrator`.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Novel, Limited Series, Short Film, Animation Feature, Documentary, Memoir | genres: Coming of Age, Heritage, Family Drama, War, Historical, Tragedy, Social Drama
**Avoid when:** There is no rupture coming, or when the rupture is meant to be a surprise. Signalling the end of the ordinary and then not ending it is a broken contract, and signalling it in a story built on surprise throws the surprise away.
**Example:**
> **Card:** *Mosul, June 2014.*
> A boy is annoyed that his mother has bought the wrong biscuits again.

**Yields to:** `open.ordinary_day_slightly_wrong` — The rupture must stay a surprise, unsignalled.  
`open.last_ordinary_day`

---

## The prologue

### The Prologue That Earns Itself

**Also called:** the justified prologue, the necessary extra beginning
**What it is:** A section before chapter one or scene one that provides something the main narrative cannot produce for itself — usually a question, a vantage point, or a fact the protagonist will never know.
**Effect on the audience:** A second layer of attention. Everything in chapter one is now being read against something.
**Used for and where it works best:** Crime, thriller, epic fantasy, historical and heritage work. The single test that decides it: does the prologue give the main story something chapter one *cannot* produce on its own? If the answer is "background", cut it. If the answer is "the reader knows the body is in the well and the family does not", keep it. Second rule: a prologue must be as strong as the best scene in the book, because it is now the book's opening, and it must contain the genre — action if the book has action, magic if the book has magic.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Limited Series, Feature Film, Game Narrative, Podcast, Animation Feature | genres: Crime, Thriller, Fantasy, Historical, Heritage, Mystery, Horror
**Avoid when:** The material is history the reader could meet later — that is `open.backstory_open` and `expo.history_prologue` with a better name. Also avoid in short forms, where the reader has no patience for two beginnings, and in most literary fiction, where the convention has largely fallen out of use.
**Example:**
> **Prologue, two pages:** a woman posts a letter she should not have written.
> **Chapter one, six years later:** her son opens his front door to a stranger holding it.

`open.prologue_earned`

### The Prologue in Another Time or Register

**Also called:** the offset prologue, the tonal step-aside, the different-voice opening
**What it is:** A prologue that is deliberately unlike the main narrative — a different century, a different narrator, a myth, a transcript, a coroner's report — so that its difference is itself the signal.
**Effect on the audience:** They read the main story looking for the join. The gap between the two registers becomes a question the book is obliged to answer.
**Used for and where it works best:** Heritage, historical, dual-timeline and literary work, and any story whose past is genuinely another world. The rule: the offset must be *large and clean*. A prologue set eighteen months earlier in the same voice reads as a misplaced chapter; a prologue set in 1917 in a found document reads as a deliberate structure. And the join must eventually arrive on the page, not merely be inferable — see `time.dual_timeline` and `time.frame_narrative`.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Limited Series, Feature Film, Documentary, Podcast, Stage Play | genres: Heritage, Historical, Literary, Mystery, War, Family Drama, Migration
**Avoid when:** The register shift is decorative. A one-page italic passage of lyrical nothing before a plain-voiced thriller is a habit, not a technique, and experienced readers skip it on sight.
**Example:**
> **Prologue:** an inventory, 1911. *Item 14: one copper tray, engraved, dented at the rim. Origin unknown.*
> **Chapter one:** a woman in a flat in Leeds, 2026, deciding whether to sell a copper tray.

`open.prologue_other_register`

### The Framing Prologue

**Also called:** the outer story, the told-tale open, the narrator's room
**What it is:** The opening establishes the situation in which the main story is being told — the interview, the trial, the deathbed, the recording, the letter — and the work then enters the story from inside that frame.
**Effect on the audience:** Certainty plus curiosity. They know someone survived to tell it, and they spend the story working out who and at what cost.
**Used for and where it works best:** Heritage, memoir adaptation, crime, testimony-based documentary, and anything where the act of telling is part of the subject. The rule that decides whether it earns its cost: the frame must have its own stakes and its own turn. A frame that is only a delivery mechanism is a tax on the opening. The strongest version returns to the frame at least once in the middle, changed, so the audience learns the telling is under pressure. See `time.frame_narrative` and `end.mirror_ending`.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Novel, Documentary, Podcast, Limited Series, Stage Play, Animation Feature | genres: Heritage, Historical, Crime, War, Literary, Family Drama, Migration
**Avoid when:** The frame reduces tension the story needs — knowing the narrator survives deflates a survival thriller. Also avoid when you cannot afford to return to it; an abandoned frame is worse than none, and it is the most common reason framing devices get cut in the edit.
**Example:**
> "State your name for the recording."
> "You know my name."
> "For the recording."
> "Then put down that I gave it under protest."

**Yields to:** `open.voiceover_open` — Cannot afford to return to the frame.  
`open.framing_prologue`

### The Prologue That Is Chapter One in Disguise

**Also called:** the relabelled first chapter, the prologue of convenience
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** A section called a prologue that is simply the story's beginning, in the same voice, the same time and the same point of view, given a different label because the writer suspected the opening was slow.
**Effect on the audience:** Nothing at first, then a specific kind of distrust when the reader realises the label meant nothing. Many readers skip anything labelled prologue, so this failure also loses the opening entirely for part of the audience.
**Used for and where it works best:** Nowhere. Listed so it can be diagnosed in a draft.
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** Always. The diagnostic is mechanical: if the prologue shares the protagonist, the time frame, the location and the voice of chapter one, it is chapter one. Rename it and renumber. The relabelling never fixed the pacing problem that prompted it — for that, apply `expo.deletion_test` to the first twenty pages instead.
**Example:**
> **Failing:** *Prologue.* Sara wakes, makes coffee, drives to work. *Chapter One.* Sara arrives at work.
> **Working:** *Chapter One.* Sara arrives at work.

**Yields to:** `open.prologue_earned` — If it must be a prologue, give what chapter one cannot.  
`open.prologue_disguised_chapter`

## Opening lines as a craft unit

### What the First Line Must Do

**Also called:** the sentence-one job list, the first-line contract
**What it is:** The specification for a first sentence: it must ground the reader somewhere, withhold something, and demonstrate the voice — three jobs in one line.
**Effect on the audience:** A decision. Most readers form a judgement about whether they are in competent hands before the end of the first sentence, and that judgement is expensive to reverse.
**Used for and where it works best:** All prose, and the first line of dialogue or narration in any script. The working balance is clarity plus curiosity: enough perceptibility that the reader is standing somewhere, enough gap that they need the next sentence. A line with clarity and no gap is a caption; a line with gap and no clarity is noise. The practical method: write the first line last, after the voice exists, and test it in isolation on someone who has not read the book.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Short Story, Memoir, Essay, Podcast, Stage Play, Pitch Document | genres: all
**Avoid when:** Never as a check — but do not let it become a paralysis. A drafted first line is a placeholder; the real one is found in revision.
**Example:**
> **No gap:** *It was the first day of my final year at school.*
> **Gap and ground:** *On the first day of my final year I was already two weeks into lying about where I lived.*

`open.first_line_job`

### The Declarative Opening

**Also called:** the flat statement, the assertion first line, the stated fact
**What it is:** The first line is a plain declarative sentence stating something as fact, with no hedging, no scene-setting and no qualification.
**Effect on the audience:** Authority. A reader granted a confident assertion assumes the writer knows the whole story and grants patience accordingly.
**Used for and where it works best:** Literary fiction, memoir, essay, narrative non-fiction and any first-person work. The craft rule: the declared fact must be *particular and slightly implausible*, so the sentence simultaneously asserts and provokes. A universal truth declared flatly reads as an epigraph; a specific odd fact declared flatly reads as a person. The variant that carries most weight is the declaration the rest of the book will complicate or disprove. See `voice.authority_by_specificity`.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Memoir, Essay, Short Story, Podcast, Pitch Document | genres: Literary, Drama, Crime, Heritage, Comedy, Social Drama, Historical
**Avoid when:** The voice elsewhere is tentative, hedged or fragmentary — a declarative first line then promises a book the reader does not get. Also avoid the version that declares a theme; that is a thesis statement, and `theme.explained_theme` covers what it costs.
**Example:**
> *My grandmother owned four houses and never once slept in a room she did not own.*

**Yields to:** `open.mid_sentence_open` — The voice elsewhere is tentative or fragmentary.  
`open.declarative_first_line`

### The Opening Question

**Also called:** the interrogative first line, the question as door
**What it is:** The work opens on a question — asked by a character, by a narrator, or rhetorically by the text itself.
**Effect on the audience:** Immediate participation. A question recruits the reader into answering, which is a different and more active state than curiosity.
**Used for and where it works best:** Essays, explainers, podcasts, first-person fiction, and any work whose structure is an investigation. In non-fiction it is close to load-bearing: an essay that names its question in the first move can spend its whole body earning the answer. In fiction the version that works is a *character's* question asked of another character, not a rhetorical one asked of the reader. Keep it to one — two questions in an opening cancel each other.
**Best in:** formats: Essay, Podcast, Explainer, Documentary, Novel, Short Story, Feature Film | genres: Literary, Journalism, Educational, Mystery, Drama, Heritage, Social Drama
**Avoid when:** The rhetorical question is one the reader can answer instantly, or answer "no" to and stop reading. *Have you ever wondered…* is the canonical dead form: it assumes an interest it has not created. In drama, avoid the narrator asking the audience anything at all.
**Example:**
> **Dead:** *Have you ever wondered how bread is made?*
> **Live:** *Why does every bakery in this city close at the same hour, and who decided it?*

**Yields to:** `open.enter_on_the_answer` — Drama, where a narrator must ask the audience nothing.  
`open.opening_question_line`

### Opening Mid-Sentence

**Also called:** the started sentence, the syntactic in medias res, the running start
**What it is:** The text begins partway through a grammatical unit — a subordinate clause, a conjunction, a continuation — so the reader arrives after the sentence has already begun.
**Effect on the audience:** The sense of having walked into a room where people were already talking. It is `time.in_medias_res` performed at the level of syntax rather than plot.
**Used for and where it works best:** Literary fiction, monologue, voice-led memoir and stage. It is the cheapest way to establish a voice with momentum, and it works especially well when the narrator is agitated, defensive or mid-argument. The rule: the reader must be able to complete the missing part from what follows within a sentence or two. If they are still reconstructing on page two, the device has become an obstacle.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Short Story, Stage Play, Memoir, Podcast, Essay, Audio Drama | genres: Literary, Comedy, Drama, Satire, Psychological, Social Drama
**Avoid when:** Genre fiction with a plot-first reader, screenplays (where action lines have a different convention), and anything read under load — instructional, technical, subtitled. Also avoid using it twice in one work; it is a signature, not a habit.
**Example:**
> *— and anyway by then the money was already gone, so what I want to explain is what I did next.*

**Yields to:** `open.declarative_first_line` — Plot-first reader or text read under load.  
`open.mid_sentence_open`

### Voice-Promising Against Plot-Promising First Lines

**Also called:** choosing the promise, the two doors
**What it is:** A choice, made deliberately: a first line either promises a *way of seeing* or promises an *event*, and the two are answered by different books and different readers.
**Effect on the audience:** They calibrate their patience. A voice promise buys slow plot; a plot promise buys thin prose. Making the wrong promise means the reader waits for something that is not coming.
**Used for and where it works best:** Every opening, as a decision to make explicitly rather than by accident. Diagnostic: read your first line and ask what the reader now expects on page thirty. If your first line promises a corpse and page thirty is a childhood memory, one of them is wrong. Literary and memoir work generally promises voice; commercial genre work generally promises plot; the hybrid — a voice line that describes an event — is the hardest to write and the most valuable when it lands. See `open.voice_hook` and `open.situation_hook` for the extended forms.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Short Story, Memoir, Feature Film, Limited Series, Pitch Document | genres: all
**Avoid when:** Never as a check. But do not let the audit produce a compromise line that promises neither — a first line that hedges between voice and plot promises nothing, which is worse than promising the wrong thing.
**Example:**
> **Voice:** *There are three ways to leave a family and my father invented a fourth.*
> **Plot:** *They found the car on Tuesday, eleven kilometres from where he said he was going.*

`open.voice_vs_plot_first_line`

### The Over-Written First Line

**Also called:** the auditioning sentence, the strained opener, purple page one
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** A first sentence written to be admired — stacked clauses, three adjectives, an ambitious metaphor — placed where the reader has no context to admire it with.
**Effect on the audience:** They notice the writer instead of the story, at the exact moment their attention is most easily lost. Agents and readers name this as the most common reason a submission is declined on page one.
**Used for and where it works best:** Nowhere. Listed so it can be diagnosed.
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** Always. The failure is not ambition, it is unearned ambition: the same sentence on page ninety, after the reader knows who is speaking and what is at stake, may be the best line in the book. The fix is relocation more often than deletion. Diagnostic: if the first sentence contains more than one image, cut it to the strongest one.
**Example:**
> **Failing:** *The morning broke over the shattered rooftops like a slow gold wound, bleeding its indifferent light across a city that had long since forgotten how to grieve.*
> **Working:** *The light came up on the rooftops. Nobody in the building was asleep.*

**Yields to:** `open.declarative_first_line` — The plain particular statement instead of the admired one.  
`open.overwritten_first_line`

---

## The first paragraph in prose

### What Belongs in the First Paragraph

**Also called:** the paragraph-one budget, the opening inventory
**What it is:** A working specification for the first paragraph: one person, one place, one unresolved thing — and no more.
**Effect on the audience:** They are standing somewhere with someone and have a reason to take a second step. That is the entire job; anything else added competes with it.
**Used for and where it works best:** All prose, and the opening block of any pitch document or essay. The hard limits, tested by how readers actually behave: at most two named people, at most one invented term, and a concrete physical anchor within the first two sentences. Everything the writer wants to add — the backstory, the second location, the third name — belongs on page four, where it costs nothing. See `expo.proper_noun_budget` and `open.overload_open`.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Short Story, Memoir, Essay, Pitch Document, Long-Form Non-Fiction | genres: all prose
**Avoid when:** A deliberately disorienting opening is the design — certain literary and science fiction work opens in confusion on purpose. Even there the limit applies to *named* things; disorientation works best when the sensory anchors are clear and only the meaning is withheld.
**Example:**
> *Sabah had been at the window since four. The van was still parked where it had been parked all week, and this morning the driver had wound the window down.*

`open.first_paragraph_contents`

### The Order of Information

**Also called:** sequencing the open, what comes first, the orientation order
**What it is:** The decision about which of place, person, action and time arrives in which sentence — a choice with predictable effects that most drafts make by accident.
**Effect on the audience:** Their attention lands where the first noun puts it. Open on a place and the story is about a place; open on a person and it is about a person; readers commit to whatever they meet first, and correcting them later costs real pages.
**Used for and where it works best:** All prose, and worth running as a deliberate pass. The default that fails least: **person, doing something, somewhere, and then when**. The variants that work are earned rather than free — time first for a historical or heritage piece where the date is the tension, place first where the place is the antagonist. The test: whichever element appears first is what you have promised the book is about. See `open.weather_open` for the standard failure of this decision.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Short Story, Memoir, Essay, Long-Form Non-Fiction, Pitch Document | genres: all prose
**Avoid when:** Never as a check. But do not mechanise it — a scene whose content genuinely is a place, arriving after fifty pages of people, is entitled to open on the place.
**Example:**
> **Place first:** *The clinic stood at the end of a road that flooded twice a year. Inside it, a nurse was arguing with a man about a form.*
> **Person first:** *The nurse had been arguing about the form for eleven minutes when the water reached the step.*

`open.information_order`

### Orientation Against Intrigue

**Also called:** the grounding-mystery balance, clarity versus pull
**What it is:** The live tension in every opening: the reader needs enough information to stand up, and too much information leaves them with no reason to move.
**Effect on the audience:** Either footing or pull, and the opening needs both. Too much orientation reads as competent and inert; too much intrigue reads as withholding and the reader disengages rather than leans in.
**Used for and where it works best:** Every opening, as the governing trade-off behind all the others. The usable ratio: orient completely on the *physical* — who, where, what is happening right now — and withhold entirely on the *causal* — why, since when, what it means. Readers tolerate almost unlimited causal mystery and almost no spatial confusion. Almost every "confusing opening" note is a spatial failure being mistaken for an intrigue problem.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Short Story, Feature Film, Limited Series, Podcast, Game Narrative, Essay | genres: all
**Avoid when:** Never as a check. The exception is deliberate disorientation in psychological and surreal work, where the spatial confusion *is* the content — and even there it usually resolves within a page.
**Example:**
> **Over-oriented:** *Zaid, forty-one, a pharmacist since 2009, divorced, was unlocking the shop he had bought from his uncle.*
> **Balanced:** *Zaid unlocked the shop at six, the way he had for eleven years, and for the first time in eleven years the alarm was already off.*

`open.orientation_vs_intrigue`

---

## Title and logline

### The Title That Changes Meaning

**Also called:** the retroactive title, the two-reading title
**What it is:** A title that means one thing before the work and a different thing after it, so that finishing the piece re-reads its own name.
**Effect on the audience:** A final small turn delivered at no cost, often after the last page. It also converts the title into a durable piece of the work rather than a label on it.
**Used for and where it works best:** Features, novels, limited series and documentary. The construction is mechanical: find the phrase whose literal reading is available up front and whose figurative reading is only available at the end, or the reverse. Titles taken from a line of dialogue work well here because the line can be planted mid-work and detonated at the close. See `theme.title_as_statement`, and place the payoff against `end.last_line`.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Novel, Limited Series, Short Film, Documentary, Stage Play, Podcast | genres: Drama, Tragedy, Crime, Literary, Heritage, War, Family Drama, Mystery
**Avoid when:** Discoverability matters more than craft — search, series branding, kids content and most short-form, where a title that means two things means neither at a glance. Also avoid when the second meaning is the twist; a title that spoils on reflection spoils on the poster.
**Example:**
> *The Good Room.* Before: the front room kept for guests. After: the only room in the house where anyone told the truth.

**Yields to:** `open.title_thumbnail_contract` — Discoverability leads: search, branding, short-form.  
`open.title_changes_meaning`

### The Logline as Diagnostic

**Also called:** the one-sentence test, the compression check
**What it is:** Writing the story as a single sentence — protagonist, goal, opposition, stakes — not to sell it, but to find out whether the story has those things at all.
**Effect on the audience:** None. This card is aimed at the writer. Its effect is on the draft.
**Used for and where it works best:** Before writing, at the midpoint, and again after the first draft — and separately for each episode of a series. The form that does the most diagnostic work: *when [inciting incident], a [flawed protagonist] must [specific goal] before [pressure], or [cost]*. Write it in one sentence; two sentences let you hide the missing element in the join. Then check it against the draft rather than against your intentions, which is where most writers' versions diverge. Pairs with `theme.controlling_idea` — the logline tests the machine, the controlling idea tests the argument.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Limited Series, One-Hour Drama, Novel, Pitch Document, Short Film, Game Narrative | genres: all
**Avoid when:** The work is not plot-driven — literary fiction, mood pieces, essay, poetry — where the compression will report a failure that is not one. For those, run the test on the *question* rather than the goal.
**Example:**
> **Vague:** *A woman deals with her family after her father's death.*
> **Diagnostic:** *When her father dies owing money to the neighbours, a woman who has not spoken to her brothers in nine years must sell the family house before the debt becomes public — or lose the only place her mother recognises.*

**Yields to:** `theme.controlling_idea` — Work that is not plot-driven; test the argument instead.  
`open.logline_diagnostic`

### Reading a Broken Logline

**Also called:** the diagnosis by absence, what the missing element means
**What it is:** Treating each element the logline cannot supply as a specific named defect in the story, rather than as a failure of summarising.
**Effect on the audience:** None directly — but every defect it finds is one the audience would have felt as boredom in act two.
**Used for and where it works best:** Development and rewriting, in features, series and long-form prose. The readings are consistent enough to be used as a table. **No active verb for the protagonist** — a passive protagonist; see `char.passive_protagonist_fix`. **No opposition** — the conflict is atmospheric and act two will sag. **No stakes clause** — nothing is at risk, only preference; see `anta.absent_stakes`. **Needing two sentences** — two stories, or a premise that only starts at the midpoint. **A logline that describes a situation rather than a change** — no arc. Do not fix the sentence. Fix the thing the sentence reported.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Limited Series, Novel, One-Hour Drama, Pitch Document, Game Narrative | genres: all
**Avoid when:** Very early drafting, where the story is legitimately still forming and premature diagnosis produces a tidy, dead outline. Run it at the end of the outline, not at the start.
**Example:**
> **Logline:** *A man returns to his village and reflects on his childhood.*
> **Reading:** no verb of intent, no opposition, no cost. This is a setting, not a story. The fix is not a better sentence — it is a reason he cannot simply leave again.

`open.broken_logline_reading`

### The Title That Promises the Wrong Genre

**Also called:** the mis-sold title, the genre mismatch at the door
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** A title whose register belongs to a different kind of work than the one it names — a playful title on a grim piece, a thriller title on a family drama, a poetic title on a procedural.
**Effect on the audience:** The wrong audience arrives and the right one never does. Those who do come feel misled, and a misled audience rates a work lower than a disappointed one.
**Used for and where it works best:** Nowhere. Listed as a named failure.
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** Always. The diagnostic is other people, not you: show the title alone to five readers and ask what kind of piece it is and what they expect to feel. If three of them name the wrong genre, the title is wrong regardless of how well it fits the theme. The same test applies to episode titles in a series, where a tonally stray title in a run of plain ones is read as a signal and generates expectations the episode does not meet.
**Example:**
> **Failing:** a documentary about the destruction of a village, titled *A Nice Place to Grow Up.* The irony is legible only after watching.
> **Working:** keep the ironic phrase as the last line on screen; title the film on its subject.

**Yields to:** `open.visual_promise` — Promise the category the piece actually belongs to.  
`open.title_genre_mismatch`

---

## Cover, thumbnail and packaging as an opening

### The Visual Promise

**Also called:** the package as first page, cover as contract, the pre-opening
**What it is:** The cover, poster, thumbnail or key art is the actual first thing the audience encounters, and it makes a promise about genre, tone and register before a single word is read.
**Effect on the audience:** A genre expectation set before the work begins, which the opening then either confirms or has to spend itself correcting. Readers and viewers absorb these visual conventions over years without being able to name them, and they treat a mismatch as dishonesty rather than as a design choice.
**Used for and where it works best:** Every published or distributed work — books, films, series, videos, podcasts, games. The craft rule: the package must speak the category's visual language and differentiate *within* it, not outside it. Standing outside the category is not boldness, it is invisibility. The second rule, more often broken: the package should promise the same thing as `open.contract_opening`, because when they disagree the audience believes the package and blames the opening.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Feature Film, Series, Reels/Shorts, Podcast, Documentary, Game Narrative | genres: all
**Avoid when:** Never as a consideration — but do not let it dictate the work. The package is the promise about the piece, not the piece. A writer who writes toward the cover produces the average of the category.
**Shelf life:** dated — review 2027-09. The specific conventions of any category's visual language move every few years; the underlying principle — the package is the first promise and must match the opening — is durable.
**Example:**
> **Mismatch:** a bright, hand-lettered cover with warm pastels on a novel about a child's disappearance. The romance reader buys it, feels ambushed, and reviews it accordingly.

`open.visual_promise`

### The Title-Thumbnail Contract

**Also called:** the packaging pair, title and image as one unit
**What it is:** In video, the title and the thumbnail are a single unit of meaning: they must not repeat each other, and together they must state one idea and leave one gap.
**Effect on the audience:** A click, or a scroll past. The pair is processed in roughly a second, and a viewer who cannot resolve what it is about in that second resolves it as "not for me".
**Used for and where it works best:** YouTube, long-form video, Shorts and Reels, and increasingly podcast episodes. The working rules, as measured across breakout videos: one subject, one message, one second to understand; high contrast against the platform's own interface colours; thumbnail text kept to about four or five words and never duplicating the title. The division of labour that works best is **thumbnail = the situation, title = the question**, or the reverse — never both doing the same job. Whatever the pair promises, the first ten seconds must deliver; see `open.first_second_hook`.
**Best in:** formats: Reels/Shorts, Explainer, Documentary, Podcast, Web Series, Vertical Micro-Drama | genres: Educational, Lifestyle, Heritage, Comedy, Journalism, Advocacy
**Avoid when:** Narrative work released as a whole, where the episode thumbnail should serve the series rather than compete per-episode. Also avoid the arms-race version — a package that over-promises raises the click and destroys the retention, which most platforms now weight against the channel.
**Shelf life:** dated — review 2027-09. The specific figures (face usage, word counts, contrast behaviour) are current 2026 platform practice and move annually. The durable part is the division of labour between the two elements.
**Example:**
> **Repeating:** Title *I Rebuilt My Grandfather's Oven.* Thumbnail text: *REBUILT THE OVEN.*
> **Paired:** Title *I Rebuilt My Grandfather's Oven.* Thumbnail: the collapsed oven, and one intact brick in a hand.

**Yields to:** `open.visual_promise` — Narrative released whole; package serves the series.  
`open.title_thumbnail_contract`

### The Package That Undersells the Work

**Also called:** the buried good piece, the invisible film
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** A strong piece given packaging that communicates nothing — a generic cover, an unreadable thumbnail, a descriptive title — so it is never opened by the people who would have liked it.
**Effect on the audience:** They never become the audience. The work is not judged badly; it is not judged.
**Used for and where it works best:** Nowhere. Listed as a named failure because it is chronically misdiagnosed as a content problem, which sends writers to rewrite work that was fine.
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** Always. The diagnostic separates the two failures cleanly: low open rate with high completion means the package is wrong; high open rate with early drop-off means the opening is wrong. Fixing the second when you have the first wastes months. The common specific causes are a thumbnail designed at full size and never checked at phone size, and a title that describes the contents instead of naming the interest.
**Shelf life:** dated — review 2027-09. The metrics named are platform-current; the underlying distinction between a packaging failure and an opening failure is durable.
**Example:**
> **Failing:** *Documentary about the School of Nisibis (Part 1)* over a wide shot of a hillside at midday.
> **Working:** *The University That Taught Europe to Read* over one carved doorway, filling the frame.

**Yields to:** `open.title_thumbnail_contract` — The packaging pair that makes the work visible.  
`open.package_undersell`

## Pitch, non-fiction and translated openings

### The First Page of a Pitch Document

**Also called:** the one-sheet, the top of the bible, the page they actually read
**What it is:** The opening page of a pitch or series bible, which must contain the entire proposition — title, logline, format, tone and engine — on the assumption that nothing after it will be read.
**Effect on the audience:** A decision about whether to continue. Commissioners and executives read the first page and stop if it does not land; everything else in the document exists to survive that first page, not to replace it.
**Used for and where it works best:** Series bibles, film pitches, commissioning documents, funding applications and grant proposals. The working contents, in order: the title; a one-sentence logline (see `open.logline_diagnostic`); the format line — length, number of episodes, register — stated flatly; the story engine, meaning what generates the next episode; and one paragraph of tone that a reader can *see*. What does not belong on page one: world history, cast lists, the writer's biography, or the theme. The test: the reader should be able to repeat your show to a colleague after page one alone. See `dial.the_pitch` for pitching it out loud.
**Best in:** formats: Pitch Document, Limited Series, One-Hour Drama, Half-Hour Comedy, Documentary, Feature Film, Game Narrative | genres: all
**Avoid when:** A commissioner has specified a different structure — house formats override craft. Also avoid opening a pitch on the theme; documents that open on what the show is *about* thematically read as undeveloped, because the engine is what gets bought.
**Example:**
> **Failing page one:** three paragraphs on the history of the neighbourhood, then the title.
> **Working page one:** the title. One line: *A retired forger is hired by the museum that prosecuted him to tell the real from the fake.* Then: 6 x 45', returnable, warm, dry, no violence.

**Yields to:** The commissioner's specified house format — House formats override craft.  
`open.pitch_first_page`

### The Documentary Open

**Also called:** the doc opening sequence, the rules of engagement
**What it is:** The documentary's first minutes, which carry the DNA of the whole film: what it is about, how it will be told, with what materials, and why it matters now.
**Effect on the audience:** A working model of the film. A documentary audience is deciding not only whether the subject interests them but whether they trust the method, and the method is only visible in the opening.
**Used for and where it works best:** Every documentary form, from a ten-minute heritage piece to a feature. The opening must declare the *elements* — if there will be reconstruction, archive, presenter, animation or interviews, the opening should contain at least one of each it intends to use, otherwise their later arrival reads as a change of programme. It must also declare the relationship between narrator and material, which is a promise the whole film is then held to; see `expo.doc_narration_contract` and `info.doc_reveal_structure`.
**Best in:** formats: Documentary, Podcast, Explainer, Limited Series, Short Film | genres: Heritage, Journalism, Historical, Social Drama, War, Nature, Educational
**Avoid when:** The film's method is itself a reveal — rare, and expensive. Also avoid the version that opens on a thesis statement; a documentary that announces its conclusion in the first minute has nothing left to do but illustrate it.
**Example:**
> A woman's hands turning over a photograph. Her voice, not a narrator's: "This is the only one left. My brother took it, and my brother is the reason there is only one."
> Then archive. The film has now shown both of its materials and its argument.

**Yields to:** `open.explainer_promise` — Name the gap rather than announce the thesis.  
`open.documentary_open`

### The Essay's First Move

**Also called:** the lede, the anecdotal opening, the way in
**What it is:** The essay begins not with its subject but with a specific small thing — a scene, a detail, an encounter — that turns out to be a doorway into the argument.
**Effect on the audience:** They agree to think about something they had not chosen to think about, because they were reading about a person and only afterwards discovered the subject.
**Used for and where it works best:** Essays, opinion writing, narrative non-fiction, long-form journalism and heritage writing. The craft rule that makes it an essay rather than a story: the specific thing must be a genuine microcosm of the general argument, and the *turn* from one to the other must be made explicitly, usually in one sentence somewhere in the third or fourth paragraph. An anecdote that never turns is a story; an argument that opens without one is a lecture. The alternative first move, equally valid, is the flat surprising fact — but it must be a fact the reader did not have.
**Best in:** formats: Essay, Long-Form Non-Fiction, Podcast, Documentary, Memoir, Explainer | genres: Journalism, Literary, Heritage, Social Drama, Historical, Educational, Advocacy
**Avoid when:** Instructional and reference writing, where the reader arrived with the question and a doorway is friction. Also avoid the exhausted forms — the dictionary definition, the famous quotation, *since the dawn of time* — all of which signal that the writer had no specific thing to start from.
**Example:**
> *My uncle kept his bakery's accounts on the back of the flour sacks. When the tax office came in 2004, he handed them a pile of sacks. What follows is not about my uncle. It is about what a state can and cannot see.*

**Yields to:** `open.stated_promise` — Instructional writing, where a doorway is friction.  
`open.essay_first_move`

### The Explainer's Promise

**Also called:** the gap named first, the question before the answer
**What it is:** An explainer opens by making the audience aware of a hole in what they know — naming the specific gap — before offering to fill it.
**Effect on the audience:** Manufactured need. A viewer who did not know they had a question cannot want the answer; an explainer that begins with the answer has nothing to hold them with.
**Used for and where it works best:** Explainers, educational video, instructional writing, heritage shorts and technical documentation. It differs from `open.stated_promise` in what is stated: the stated promise names the deliverable, this names the *deficit*. The strongest version uses something the audience already believes and shows it is incomplete, because correcting a belief is more compelling than acquiring a fact. Then deliver in the order promised — an explainer that reorders its own promise loses the audience at the first mismatch. See `expo.explainer_scaffold`.
**Best in:** formats: Explainer, Documentary, Podcast, Reels/Shorts, Essay, Animation | genres: Educational, Journalism, Heritage, Historical, Advocacy, Lifestyle
**Avoid when:** The audience already has the question — a reader searching for how to do something wants step one, not a preamble explaining why they want it. Also avoid the manufactured-ignorance version, where the gap is invented and the audience knows it; that costs trust for the whole piece.
**Example:**
> *You have seen this arch a hundred times and you have almost certainly been told the wrong century. Here is how we know, and here is who benefited from the wrong date.*

**Yields to:** `open.stated_promise` — Audience already has the question; name the deliverable.  
`open.explainer_promise`

### The Opening Under Subtitles

**Also called:** the translated open, the read opening, the first subtitle
**What it is:** Writing an opening for an audience that will be reading it — where the first minutes must survive being processed as text at the bottom of the frame rather than as speech.
**Effect on the audience:** Split attention, at the exact moment attention is most fragile. Subtitles pull the eye downward and away from peripheral action, and a subtitled opening asks for a greater level of effort than the same opening dubbed or native.
**Used for and where it works best:** Any work with an international release, heritage and Arabic-language work released in English, and all burned-caption social video. The practical rules: keep the first minute's line count low and the lines short; do not place plot-critical information in overlapping dialogue at the opening, because only one line can be read at a time; and never put a crucial visual detail in the lower third of the frame in the first minutes. Compensate with image — a subtitled opening should lean harder on `open.object_opening` and `open.scale_reveal` than a native-language one. See `dial.subtitle_constraint` and `rhythm.subtitle_beat`.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Documentary, Limited Series, Reels/Shorts, Vertical Micro-Drama, Short Film, Animation Feature | genres: Heritage, Historical, War, Social Drama, Drama, Crime, Migration
**Avoid when:** The work will be dubbed as its primary release, where the constraint is lip-sync rather than reading speed and the opposite advice applies. Also do not let it flatten the dialogue: the answer is fewer lines in the opening, not simpler ones.
**Example:**
> **Failing open:** four characters talking over each other about a land dispute, six subtitle lines in twenty seconds.
> **Working open:** one man reading a document aloud, slowly, to a woman who already knows what it says.

**Yields to:** `rhythm.lip_sync_adaptation` — Dubbed as primary release; lip-sync, not reading speed.  
`open.subtitled_open`

## Openings in interactive work

### The Tutorial That Is a Scene

**Also called:** diegetic onboarding, teaching inside the fiction
**What it is:** The opening teaches the player how to play while being an actual scene — the mechanics are learned through an action the character has a reason to take.
**Effect on the audience:** They are inside the story from the first input rather than after it. A tutorial outside the fiction makes the first ten minutes a manual, and the story then has to start twice.
**Used for and where it works best:** Game narrative, interactive fiction and XR. The rule: every mechanic taught in the opening needs an in-world reason to be performed now, and the character's want supplies it. The strongest version teaches the mechanic on a *low-stakes* version of the thing the game is actually about, so the player learns the verb and the theme at once. Mismatch here is expensive: a tutorial that teaches violence in a game arguing against violence is `inter.ludonarrative_dissonance` introduced at minute one, where it does the most damage.
**Best in:** formats: Game Narrative, Interactive Fiction, Animation, Explainer | genres: Adventure, Science Fiction, Horror, Drama, Heritage, Mystery, Social Drama
**Avoid when:** The systems are genuinely complex and gating them behind fiction makes them unlearnable — some games are better served by an optional explicit tutorial plus a clean narrative opening. Also avoid for the returning player: see `inter.skippable_layering`.
**Example:**
> The first thing the player is taught is how to carry two objects at once. They are taught it by a mother handing them a child and a bag at a checkpoint.

**Yields to:** `inter.skippable_layering` — The returning player, or systems too complex to gate.  
`open.tutorial_as_scene`

### The First Choice

**Also called:** the opening decision, the agency handshake
**What it is:** The first decision the work asks the player or reader to make, which establishes what kind of choices this work contains and how much they will matter.
**Effect on the audience:** A calibration of trust. The first choice teaches whether decisions here are characterisation, consequence or decoration, and players read the answer fast and act on it for the rest of the piece.
**Used for and where it works best:** Interactive fiction, game narrative, branching video and choice-based mobile drama. The rule: make the first choice *small in stakes and visibly acknowledged*. A trivial choice that the work clearly remembers builds more trust than a large choice that visibly changes nothing. Never open on the piece's biggest decision — the player has no basis to make it and will resent the result. See `inter.meaningful_choice_test`, `inter.flavour_choice` and `inter.illusion_of_agency`.
**Best in:** formats: Interactive Fiction, Game Narrative, Vertical Micro-Drama, Web Series | genres: Drama, Mystery, Science Fiction, Horror, Romance, Adventure, Social Drama
**Avoid when:** The work's design is a single authored path with flavour choices only — then an opening choice that looks consequential is a lie told at the door, and everything after is read through it. Better to open on a flavour choice that is honestly framed as self-expression.
**Example:**
> Before anything else: *Do you take the photograph off the wall, or leave it?*
> Two hours later, a character mentions that the wall looks bare.

**Yields to:** `inter.flavour_choice` — Single authored path; an honest self-expression choice.  
`open.first_choice`

## More named failures

### The Opening That Promises a Different Piece

**Also called:** the bait opening, the borrowed first act, the mis-set expectation
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** An opening written in the register of a more marketable or more exciting work than the one that follows — an action sequence on a chamber drama, a comic first chapter on a grief novel, a horror teaser on a mystery.
**Effect on the audience:** They spend the first act waiting for a piece that is not coming, and they experience the actual piece as a disappointment rather than on its own terms. The work is then judged against the wrong standard for its whole length.
**Used for and where it works best:** Nowhere. Note the deliberate tonal swerve is a different technique — see the exception in `open.contract_opening` — and it is defined by paying the mismatch off explicitly, not by abandoning it.
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** Always. The diagnostic: describe your opening in one sentence and your work in one sentence, and show both to someone who has read neither. If they do not believe the two belong together, the opening is borrowed. It is usually borrowed out of anxiety about the real opening being quiet — the repair is to make the quiet opening specific, not to attach a louder one.
**Example:**
> **Failing:** a novel about a marriage opening with a car crash that turns out to be unrelated and unmentioned again.
> **Working:** the same novel opening on the argument they have in the car, ten minutes before the junction.

**Yields to:** `open.contract_opening` — The deliberate swerve that pays the mismatch off.  
`open.wrong_promise`

### The Wrong Character First

**Also called:** the front-loaded minor character, the false protagonist by accident
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** The opening spends its attention on someone who is not the story's centre — a narrator's parent, a victim, a mentor, a colleague — and the audience attaches to them before the protagonist arrives.
**Effect on the audience:** Misdirected attachment, which is very hard to reverse. Readers bond with whoever they meet first, and asking them to transfer that to a character introduced on page twenty is a cost paid for the rest of the work.
**Used for and where it works best:** Nowhere as an accident. The deliberate version — a false protagonist who is deliberately removed — is a different technique and requires the removal to be the story's first major event, not a quiet fade.
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** Always, unless designed. The diagnostic: ask a reader who the book is about after page ten. If they name the wrong person, either move the protagonist forward or accept the answer and rewrite the book around it — the second option is right more often than writers expect. Note that a prologue centred on a minor character produces this failure even when the main narrative is correctly centred.
**Example:**
> **Failing:** eight pages with the retiring detective, then the story hands over to the junior officer it is actually about.
> **Working:** open on the junior officer watching the retirement, wanting something from it.

`open.wrong_character_first`

### The Device Used Once

**Also called:** the abandoned frame, the orphan device, the one-off conceit
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** An opening that introduces a formal device — a dream, a narrator, a direct address, an on-screen text convention, a second timeline, a found document — which the work never uses again.
**Effect on the audience:** A structural itch. The audience holds the device open, waiting for its return, and when it never comes they retroactively read it as a mistake — which teaches them to discount the work's other formal choices.
**Used for and where it works best:** Nowhere. This is the failure that swallows the largest number of otherwise good openings, because openings are where writers experiment most and revise least.
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** Always. The rule is arithmetic: any device introduced in an opening must appear at least twice more, and one of those appearances should be near the end. If it cannot, cut it from the opening — the opening will be plainer and the work will be more coherent. Dreams are the most frequent offender, closely followed by narration added in post; see `open.false_start` and `open.voiceover_open`.
**Example:**
> **Failing:** the film opens with a character speaking to camera. Nobody speaks to camera again for ninety minutes.
> **Working:** the same address opens the film, returns at the midpoint with the character now lying, and closes the film in silence with the character looking at the lens and saying nothing.

**Yields to:** `info.plant_and_payoff` — Any opening device must return, twice, one near the end.  
`open.abandoned_device`

Dated cards in this part: `open.visual_promise`, `open.title_thumbnail_contract` and `open.package_undersell`, all reviewed 2027-09, because they rest on platform and market convention rather than on craft. Everything else is durable.
